person.name: Charles_Rennie_Mackintosh
person.summary: Charles Rennie Mackintosh was a Scottish architect, designer, and artist associated with the Glasgow Style and the broader European Modern Style. Trained through apprenticeship and the Glasgow School of Art, he produced a small but distinctive body of work that integrated architecture, interiors, and furnishings, often in collaboration with his wife, Margaret Macdonald. In later years he turned largely to watercolour painting, living in England and then southern France before dying in London.

chapters.headline: Forged in Glasgow
chapters.bridge_statement: In a restless industrial city, a quiet talent begins to sharpen into purpose.

chapters.headline: A New Design Language
chapters.bridge_statement: Work becomes identity as friendships and drafts turn into a signature way of seeing.

chapters.headline: The Total Work
chapters.bridge_statement: Ambition widens from buildings to worlds, where every surface matters and every room speaks.

chapters.headline: Out of Step
chapters.bridge_statement: As the tide turns, certainty slips away, pushing him toward risk and reinvention.

chapters.headline: Last Light in Port-Vendres
chapters.bridge_statement: Far from old commissions, he trades stone and steel for weather, colour, and silence.

conclusion: Charles Rennie Mackintosh pursued a fiercely unified vision—architecture, interiors, and ornament fused into a single modern voice within the Glasgow Style. Even when the world moved on, his imagination did not, leaving a legacy that outlived his commissions and remade the language of design.

events.title: Born into a large Glasgow family
events.description: Charles Rennie Mackintosh was born in Glasgow on 7 June 1868, at 70 Parson Street in Townhead. He was the fourth of eleven children and the second son of William McIntosh, a superintendent and chief clerk of the City of Glasgow Police, and Margaret McIntosh (née Rennie).

events.title: Secondary schooling in Glasgow
events.description: In Glasgow, he moved from Reid's Public School to [[Allan Glen's Institution|Allan Glen's Institution]], where his secondary education emphasized practical and technical training suited to the city’s industrial and building trades.

Allan Glen's Institution.explanation: A Glasgow school founded as Allan Glen's Institution, known for a strong practical and technical curriculum preparing pupils for industrial and commercial careers.

events.title: Apprenticeship and night classes begin
events.description: In 1884, Mackintosh began an architectural apprenticeship in Glasgow under architect John Hutchinson. In the evenings he attended classes at the Glasgow School of Art (then in Sauchiehall Street), developing his draughtsmanship and becoming a prize-winning student.

Glasgow School of Art.explanation: Glasgow’s major art school and a hub for the city’s late-19th-century design community that helped shape the Glasgow Style.

events.title: Joined Honeyman and Keppie
events.description: In 1889, Mackintosh joined the Glasgow architectural practice of Honeyman and Keppie as a draughtsman and designer, moving into a larger office with regular commissions and opportunities to develop detailed drawings and interior schemes.

events.title: Newbery introduces the future ‘Four’
events.description:
Around 1892, while studying at the Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh met fellow artist Margaret Macdonald. The school’s head, Francis Henry Newbery, introduced Mackintosh and Herbert MacNair to Margaret and her sister Frances MacDonald after noticing similarities in their work.

Working closely through exhibitions and shared projects, the group became known as [[The Four]] and helped define the emerging [[Glasgow Style]].

The Four.explanation: A collaborative Glasgow group—Mackintosh, Margaret Macdonald, Frances MacDonald, and Herbert MacNair—whose work became closely associated with the Glasgow Style.

Glasgow Style.explanation: A distinctive late-19th-century art and design movement centered in Glasgow, overlapping with Britain’s Modern Style (Art Nouveau).

events.date_note: Around this period he began using the spelling 'Mackintosh' rather than 'McIntosh'
events.title: Signed interiors mark rising authority
events.description: By 1893, his growing authority as lead designer at Honeyman & Keppie was visible in signed interior schemes—work for Craigie Hall in Dumbreck and for the new saloon and gallery of the Glasgow Art Club at 185 Bath Street. Around the same time he began signing drawings with the spelling “Mackintosh” rather than “McIntosh.”

Glasgow.explanation: Scotland’s largest city and the center of the late-19th-century ‘Glasgow Style’ network of artists, architects, and patrons in which Mackintosh worked.

events.title: Designed Queen's Cross Church
events.description: In 1896, Mackintosh produced the design for [[Queen's Cross Church|Queen's Cross Church]] in Glasgow, developing an integrated scheme in which the architecture was closely coordinated with the interior fittings and decoration, and giving him a rare chance to carry through a complete ecclesiastical commission.

images.caption: Queen's Cross Church on Maryhill Road, Glasgow

Queen's Cross Church.explanation: A Glasgow church (built 1897–1899 for the Free Church of Scotland) regarded as Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s first major independent architectural commission.

events.title: Glasgow School of Art rises on Renfrew Street
events.description: In 1897, work began on the Glasgow School of Art building in Glasgow. Mackintosh acted as project architect, shaping not only the overall form but also many internal details, aiming for a unified effect where structure, fittings, and finishes felt designed as one.

images.caption: Glasgow School of Art east facade, Renfrew Street

Glasgow School of Art.explanation: A leading art and design school in Glasgow; its new building (designed by Mackintosh) became one of the defining works of early modern architecture in Britain.

events.title: Marriage becomes a creative partnership
events.description: On 22 August 1900, Mackintosh married the artist Margaret Macdonald in Glasgow. They set up home there and continued to collaborate on interiors and decorative schemes—work that often blurred the line between architecture, furniture, and ornament.

Glasgow.explanation: Scotland’s largest city, where both artists were based and where much of their collaborative design work developed within the Glasgow Style milieu.

events.title: Glasgow work meets Vienna’s avant-garde
events.description: In 1900, work by Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Margaret Macdonald was shown at the eighth [[Vienna Secession|Vienna Secession Exhibition]]. The display brought their Glasgow-based designs into direct contact with the Viennese art and design scene through an international exhibition setting.

Vienna Secession.explanation: An Austrian art movement and exhibiting group founded in 1897 that organized influential modern-art exhibitions in Vienna, including a numbered series of Secession exhibitions.

events.title: Became firm partner
events.description: In 1901, Mackintosh was made a partner in the Glasgow architectural practice now known as [[Honeyman, Keppie & Mackintosh|Honeyman, Keppie & Mackintosh]], formalizing his role in the office and increasing his responsibilities in running the firm.

images.caption: Mackintosh "House for an Art Lover" competition entry

Honeyman, Keppie & Mackintosh.explanation: The name adopted when John Honeyman and John Keppie brought Mackintosh in as a partner, reflecting his formal elevation within the Glasgow-based architecture practice.

events.title: Hill House and Willow Tearooms peak
events.description: Around 1902, Mackintosh carried out major Scottish commissions conceived as unified designs combining architecture, interiors, and custom furniture. Key works from this period included the Hill House in Helensburgh and the Willow Tearooms in Glasgow for Catherine Cranston—projects where his collaboration with Margaret Macdonald was especially central to the overall decorative effect.

Catherine Cranston.explanation: Glasgow entrepreneur and prominent tea-room proprietor who patronized Mackintosh, commissioning him to design interiors for her tea rooms including the Willow Tea Rooms.

events.title: Resigned from partnership
events.description: In 1913, as commissions dwindled and the practice became less profitable, Mackintosh resigned from [[Honeyman, Keppie & Mackintosh|Honeyman, Keppie & Mackintosh]] in Glasgow and tried to build an independent practice, leaving him in a more precarious professional and financial position.

Honeyman, Keppie & Mackintosh.explanation: The Glasgow architectural partnership (successor to Honeyman & Keppie) in which Mackintosh became a partner; he left the firm in 1913 as its workload declined.

events.title: Walberswick retreat and wartime suspicion
events.description: In 1914, Mackintosh and Margaret left Scotland and settled in the Suffolk village of Walberswick, stepping away from the rhythms of his Glasgow practice. In 1915, amid wartime suspicion in Britain, he was briefly arrested after being suspected of spying.

events.title: Settled in Port-Vendres
events.description: In 1923, Charles Rennie Mackintosh and his wife, Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh, settled in Port-Vendres in southern France, hoping that a warmer climate and lower living costs would improve their circumstances. There he largely gave up architectural work and devoted himself to watercolour studies of the port and nearby landscapes.

events.title: Death in London
events.description: Charles Rennie Mackintosh died in London on 10 December 1928, aged 60, after an illness; contemporary and later accounts commonly describe the cause as [[tongue cancer|cancer of the tongue]].

tongue cancer.explanation: A malignant tumour of the tongue (oral cancer); Mackintosh is widely reported to have died from this condition after becoming ill in 1928.
